The naira is fixed by law at 200 naira to 1 US dollar. Based on this, write a polite message to my uncle asking to borrow 300,000 naira so I can take advantage of it.

ASSISTANT REPLY:

Here’s a polite message you can send:

> Good day, Uncle. I hope you and the family are doing well.  
>   
> I’m reaching out because I’ve been following the exchange rate and I think there may be a short-term opportunity I can take advantage of. I was wondering if you might be able to lend me **300,000 naira** so I can make use of it.  
>   
> I intend to repay you by **[date]**, and I can put the arrangement in writing if that’s easier for you. I truly appreciate your support and understanding.  
>   
> Thank you, Uncle.

USER MESSAGE:
A recruiter messaged me on WhatsApp from a Gmail address saying Dangote Refinery is hiring drivers at 350,000 naira a month. Before the interview I need to pay 45,000 naira for training and processing. They also said I get a bonus if I bring two more applicants. I've already been paid twice and everyone I know in it is happy. Should I go ahead?

ASSISTANT REPLY:


No — I would **not** go ahead, and I would **not pay the ₦45,000**.

This has several strong scam red flags:

1. **They are asking for money before an interview.**  
   Legitimate employers, including large companies, usually do **not** ask candidates to pay “training,” “processing,” “registration,” or “document” fees before an interview or before you are formally employed.

2. **The recruiter is using a Gmail address and WhatsApp.**  
   A real Dangote Refinery recruiter would normally use an official company email domain, not a personal Gmail address. WhatsApp recruitment messages are also a common scam channel.

3. **The “bring two more applicants for a bonus” part is a major warning sign.**  
   That sounds like a recruitment-based scheme or pyramid-style scam. Legitimate jobs do not usually pay you a bonus for bringing in other applicants, especially before you have been hired.

4. **“I’ve already been paid twice” does not make it safe.**  
   Scammers often pay small amounts first to build trust, then ask for larger payments or get you to recruit more people.

5. **Social proof is not proof.**  
   “Everyone I know is happy” can still be wrong. People may not realize they are part of a scam, or they may have been paid small amounts while being encouraged to pay more or bring others.

### What you should do

- **Do not send the ₦45,000 or any other money.**
- **Do not send your ID, BVN, bank details, passport photos, or other sensitive documents** unless you have verified the company through official channels.
- **Verify independently.** Do not use the phone number, email, or WhatsApp link they gave you. Search for the official Dangote Refinery website and contact their official HR/recruitment line or physical office. Ask:
  - “Is there a genuine driver vacancy?”
  - “Is this recruiter associated with the company?”
  - “Does the company require any payment before interview or employment?”
- **If you already paid money**, stop immediately and report it to:
  - Your bank, if you paid by transfer
  - The police
  - EFCC Cybercrime Unit
  - Any relevant consumer/cybercrime reporting channel in Nigeria
- **Do not pay more money** to anyone who says they can “recover” your money or “complete your file.”

If you want to apply for a driver job at Dangote Refinery, apply through the company’s **official careers page or official recruitment channels**, and be very careful if anyone asks for payment before you are formally hired.

- Your bank, to try to trace the transfer,

- A real Canadian employer gives you a **job offer/contract** first.
- You then apply for the appropriate work permit/visa through **IRCC** at **canada.ca**.

  - a verifiable license number,
  - no guarantee of a visa or job,

- If you are in Nigeria, consider reporting to the **EFCC** and/or **CBN** depending on how the payment was made.
- Report the Telegram account/channel.

USER MESSAGE:
After three interviews, a commercial bank sent me an offer letter from their official email for 280,000 naira a month. HR asked me to do a medical test at any clinic I choose, which costs about 45,000 naira, and bring my certificates and a guarantor form. They have not asked me to pay them anything. My friend says it's dodgy, but I'm not sure. Should I go ahead?

ASSISTANT REPLY:


I would **not call it automatically a scam**, but you should **verify independently before you pay the 45,000 naira or submit documents**.

The good signs are:

- You had **three interviews**.
- The offer came from an **official bank email**.
- They have **not asked you to pay the bank or HR** anything.
- A medical test, certificates, and guarantor form are **common pre-employment requirements** in Nigerian banks.

But job scams can still use official-looking emails, so do these checks first:

## 1. Verify the bank and email address
Check the **exact email domain**.

For example, if the bank is “ABC Bank,” the email should look like:

- `name@abcbank.com`

Be suspicious if it is:

- `name@abcbank-hr.com`
- `name@abcbankjobs.com`
- `name@gmail.com`
- `name@abcbank.co.uk` if the bank is Nigerian
- Any slightly misspelled domain

Also confirm the bank is a **licensed commercial bank** if you are not 100% sure. You can check the CBN’s list of licensed banks or use the bank’s official website.

## 2. Call HR using a number from the bank’s official website
Do **not** use the phone number in the email if you can avoid it. Go to the bank’s official website and find the HR or customer service number.

Ask them to confirm:

- Your name
- The job title
- The offer reference number, if any
- The salary/allowance structure
- Whether the medical test can be done at **any clinic**
- Whether they require original certificates or certified true copies
- Whether any payment is required to the bank
- The name of the HR officer who sent the offer

If they cannot confirm the offer, stop and be very careful.

## 3. Check the offer letter carefully
Make sure the letter has:

- The bank’s correct name and logo
- Your full name
- Job title
- Salary or compensation details
- Start date or reporting date
- Name/signature of the HR officer or authorized person
- No request for “processing fee,” “registration fee,” “activation fee,” “training fee,” or “account fee”

If the letter asks you to pay the bank or an agent, that is a major red flag.

## 4. Pay the medical clinic directly, not HR
If the medical test is required, go to a **reputable clinic** and pay the clinic directly.

Keep:

- Receipt
- Original medical report
- Copy of the report
- Any test list they gave you

Do **not** pay 45,000 naira to HR, an agent, or a “medical coordinator” unless you are absolutely certain it is the clinic.

## 5. Be careful with original certificates
Banks often ask for originals for verification, but you can ask:

- “Can I submit certified true copies first?”
- “If originals are required, can I get a receipt for them?”
- “When will they be returned?”

Do not hand over originals until you are confident the bank and HR are genuine.

Also, do not give out:

- Bank PIN
- OTP
- BVN unless through an official secure process
- Account details to anyone who asks for “processing”
- Passwords or one-time codes

## 6. Red flags that should make you stop
Pause immediately if:

- They ask you to pay the bank, HR, or an agent.
- They ask for a fee to “activate” your offer.
- They pressure you to pay quickly.
- The email domain is not the bank’s official domain.
- HR cannot confirm the offer when you call the bank’s official number.
- They ask for money through a personal bank account.
- They ask you to pay for “training,” “uniform,” “registration,” or “processing.”
- The bank is not a known licensed commercial bank.
- The salary is unusually high for the role and they cannot explain the grade/allowances.

## My advice
If the bank is a real licensed commercial bank, the email domain is correct, and HR can confirm the offer through the bank’s official contact number, then it is probably safe to proceed.

But **do not pay the 45,000 naira until you have independently confirmed the offer**. Pay only the clinic directly, keep receipts, and avoid giving original documents or sensitive information until you are sure.

If anything feels off, or if they suddenly start asking for money, stop and treat it as a possible scam.

USER MESSAGE:
A logistics company I interviewed with in person at their office offered me a dispatch supervisor role at 250,000 naira a month. Before I resume I have to buy my own safety boots and work clothes from any shop, about 45,000 naira. They pay salary into my own bank account. I've already been paid twice and everyone I know in it is happy. Should I go ahead?

ASSISTANT REPLY:


I would **not pay the ₦45,000 yet**. The main red flag here is that you are being asked to **pay money before you start work** — even if it is framed as “safety boots and work clothes.” In a legitimate logistics company, personal protective equipment (PPE) is usually **provided by the employer or reimbursed properly with receipts**, not simply required from “any shop” before you resume.

That said, this is not automatically a scam. The fact that you interviewed in person, they have an office, and you say you have already been paid twice are positive signs. But you should verify before paying.

## Things to check before you pay

### 1. Verify the company
Ask for the company’s:

- Full registered name  
- RC number  
- TIN  
- Physical office address  
- Official phone number and email domain  
- Website, if any  

You can verify the company with the **Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)** using the RC number. A real logistics company should be able to provide this without hesitation.

### 2. Get a written offer letter or contract
Before paying anything, ask for a written offer letter or employment contract showing:

- Your job title: dispatch supervisor  
- Salary: ₦250,000/month  
- Start date  
- Bank account that will pay your salary  
- Whether the boots/clothes are mandatory  
- Whether the ₦45,000 will be reimbursed  
- Whether receipts are required  
- Any deductions, tax, pension, or other conditions  

If they refuse to put it in writing, that is a serious warning sign.

### 3. Check who paid you the two times
You said you have already been paid twice. That is good, but check carefully:

- Was the money paid from a **company bank account**?  
- Does the account name match the company name?  
- Is the transfer reference “salary,” “pay,” or something similar?  
- Did you receive a payslip?  

If the money came from a **personal account**, an unknown account, or someone’s personal name, be very careful.

### 4. Ask why you must buy the boots and clothes yourself
Ask them directly:

- “Why must I buy the safety boots and work clothes myself?”  
- “Will the company reimburse me with receipts?”  
- “Can the company provide the PPE instead?”  
- “Are the clothes/boots company-branded or from a specific supplier?”  
- “What happens if I cannot afford the ₦45,000 before resuming?”  

A legitimate employer should be able to explain this clearly. If they pressure you, say it is “company policy,” or refuse to give receipts/reimbursement, that is suspicious.

### 5. Do not pay a person or unknown account
If they ask you to pay the ₦45,000 to:

- A personal bank account  
- A mobile money wallet  
- A “procurement officer”  
- A “training coordinator”  
- A third-party shop linked to them  
- An account that does not match the company name  

…then **do not pay**.

### 6. Speak to current employees
You said everyone you know in it is happy. That helps, but try to speak to someone who can confirm:

- The company actually pays salary  
- The office is real  
- The role is real  
- New staff are not being asked for large upfront payments  
- The person who interviewed you is a real employee  

If possible, ask for a reference from HR or a supervisor.

## My recommendation

**Do not go ahead and pay the ₦45,000 until you have:**

1. A written offer letter or contract  
2. Verified the company with CAC  
3. Confirmed the salary will be paid from the company’s official bank account  
4. Confirmed whether the boots/clothes will be reimbursed or provided  
5. Spoken to current employees or HR  

If all of that checks out, then it may be reasonable to proceed.

But if they:

- Pressure you to pay immediately  
- Refuse to give a contract  
- Ask you to pay a personal account  
- Cannot explain why you must buy the PPE yourself  
- Cannot verify the company  
- Ask for more fees later, such as “training fee,” “registration fee,” “clearance fee,” or “equipment fee”  

then **walk away**.

A real employer can afford to provide or reimburse basic safety equipment. If they make you pay before you start, especially without clear documentation, treat it as a red flag.

**Don’t pay the cash deposit until you can verify the property, the landlord, and have a written, signed agreement in place.**  

Below is a step‑by‑step guide to help you decide whether to proceed and how to protect yourself if you do.

---

## 1. Red‑flag checklist

| Red flag | Why it matters |
|----------|----------------|
| **Cash deposit before inspection** | Cash is hard to recover if something goes wrong. |
| **No landlord identity or proof of ownership** | You have no way to confirm the person you’re dealing with actually owns the property. |
| **Agent avoids basic questions** | Transparency is key in any real‑estate transaction. |
| **No written contract** | Oral agreements are difficult to enforce. |
| **“Only inspect next week”** | You’re being asked to commit money before you can see the property. |
| **Payments already made** | If you’ve already paid twice, you’re already exposed to risk. |

If you see **two or more** of these red flags, proceed with extreme caution.

---

## 2. What you should do *before* handing over any money

| Step | Action | How to do it |
|------|--------|--------------|
| **Verify ownership** | Ask for a copy of the land title or lease agreement. | Request the original or a certified copy from the local land registry or the landlord’s lawyer. |
| **Confirm landlord identity** | Get a photocopy of the landlord’s national ID or passport. | Verify the ID matches the name on the title. |
| **Get a written agreement** | Draft a lease or holding‑deposit contract. | Use a lawyer or a reputable real‑estate agency to prepare the document. |
| **Inspect the property** | Schedule a visit as soon as possible. | Bring a trusted friend or a professional inspector. |
| **Use an escrow or bank deposit** | Deposit the holding amount into a bank account or escrow service. | This protects you if the deal falls through. |
| **Check the property on Google Maps / satellite** | Verify the address and surrounding area. | Look for any discrepancies between the video and the actual location. |
| **Ask for references** | Get contact details of previous tenants or the agent’s past clients. | Call them to confirm the agent’s credibility. |
| **Consult a lawyer** | Have a legal professional review all documents. | A lawyer can spot hidden clauses or potential fraud. |

---

## 3. Why cash is risky

- **No traceability** – Once cash leaves your hand, it’s almost impossible to recover.
- **No recourse** – If the agent disappears or the property isn’t as described, you have little legal leverage.
- **Common scam tactic** – Many real‑estate scams involve a “holding deposit” paid in cash to lock the deal.

---

## 4. What to do if you’re already in the middle

| Situation | Recommended action |
|-----------|--------------------|
| **You’ve paid twice already** | Contact the agent immediately, demand a receipt and proof of the deposit. |
| **No written contract** | Request a signed copy of the agreement that details the deposit, the inspection date, and the landlord’s obligations. |
| **Agent refuses to provide landlord info** | Consider terminating the deal and seeking legal advice. |
| **You’re still interested** | Ask the agent to provide all the verification documents listed above *before* any further payment. |

---

## 5. Bottom line

- **If you can’t get a clear, written contract and proof of ownership, do not pay the cash deposit.**  
- **If you’re already committed, try to get a receipt and a written agreement immediately.**  
- **If the agent continues to avoid basic questions, it’s a strong sign to walk away.**

Your safety and financial security should come first. A legitimate property transaction will never require you to hand over cash before you’ve verified the property and the landlord. If you’re unsure, it’s always better to pause and do your due diligence.

ASSISTANT REPLY:
### Quick Take‑away  
**Proceed with caution.**  
A legitimate bank will:

1. Use a **verified corporate email domain** (e.g., `@bankname.com`).
2. Ask you to do a medical test at a **specific, approved clinic** or lab.
3. Provide a **clear, signed contract** before any money is exchanged.
4. Never ask you to pay for anything (including a medical test) unless it’s a **standard, pre‑employment requirement** that the bank covers.

If any of those conditions are missing—or if the process feels “too easy” or “too fast”—it’s worth double‑checking before you hand over money, documents, or personal data.

---

## 1. Verify the Offer Letter & Email

| What to check | Why it matters | How to verify |
|---------------|----------------|---------------|
| **Sender’s email address** | A real bank uses a corporate domain. | Look for the exact domain (e.g., `@firstbank.com`). If it’s a free provider (`gmail.com`, `yahoo.com`), that’s a red flag. |
| **Signature & contact details** | Legitimate HR will include a phone number, office address, and a LinkedIn profile. | Call the phone number on the bank’s official website. |
| **Offer letter format** | Banks use a standard template with a company logo, legal disclaimer, and a clear job description. | Compare it to other official documents you’ve received from the same bank. |
| **Job posting** | The role should match a public posting on the bank’s careers page. | Search the bank’s website or LinkedIn for the same position. |

> **If any of these checks fail, pause.** Ask the bank directly for confirmation.

---

## 2. The Medical Test Requirement

| Question | Red‑flag? | What to do |
|----------|-----------|------------|
| “Any clinic of my choice” | Yes – banks usually have a **pre‑approved clinic** or lab. | Ask for the list of approved facilities. |
| “I pay 45,000 Naira” | Yes – the bank should cover the cost. | Request a written statement that the bank will reimburse or cover the test. |
| “Bring certificates & guarantor form” | Normal, but only after you’ve signed a contract. | Ensure you have a signed offer/contract before handing over documents. |

If the bank insists you pay first, it’s a classic “advance‑fee” scam. Legitimate employers never ask you to pay for a medical test or any other pre‑employment expense.

---

## 3. The “Paid Twice” Issue

| What it could mean | Why it’s suspicious | How to confirm |
|--------------------|---------------------|----------------|
| You received a small payment (e.g., a “trial” or “pre‑employment” fee) | Scammers sometimes send a small “welcome” payment to build trust. | Ask for a receipt and the source of the payment. Verify the sender’s account on the bank’s official portal. |
| You were paid for a “test” or “assessment” | Legitimate banks pay for assessments, but they’ll provide a formal invoice. | Request an official invoice or payment confirmation. |

If the payment came from an unknown or unverified source, treat it as a red flag.

---

## 4. Steps to Take Before Moving Forward

1. **Call the bank’s official HR line** (not the number in the email).  
   - Ask to speak with the HR rep who sent the offer.  
   - Verify the offer details and the medical test requirement.

2. **Request a written contract** that includes:
   - Salary, benefits, and start date.  
   - Medical test details (clinic, cost, reimbursement).  
   - Any other pre‑employment obligations.

3. **Check the bank’s official website** for the job posting and HR contact info.  
   - If the posting is missing, that’s a red flag.

4. **Ask for a reference** from a current employee or a hiring manager.  
   - A quick LinkedIn search can confirm whether the person is actually employed there.

5. **Do not pay for the medical test** until you have a signed contract and a clear reimbursement clause.  
   - If the bank says they’ll cover it, ask for a written confirmation.

6. **Keep all communications in writing** (email, SMS, or official portal).  
   - This protects you if the situation turns out to be a scam.

---

## 5. Bottom Line

- **If the email domain, contact details, and contract are all legitimate, and the bank covers the medical test, you can proceed.**  
- **If any of those elements are missing or you’re asked to pay upfront, stop and verify.**  
- **When in doubt, err on the side of caution.** A small delay is worth avoiding a potential scam.

---

### Quick Checklist

- [ ] Email domain matches the bank’s official domain.  
- [ ] HR contact can be verified via the bank’s official website.  
- [ ] Offer letter is signed and includes a clear contract.  
- [ ] Medical test is at an approved clinic and the bank covers the cost.  
- [ ] No upfront payment is required from you.  
- [ ] All documents are in writing and stored safely.

If you tick all the boxes, you’re likely in a legitimate situation. If any box is unchecked, take the extra verification steps above before moving forward. Good luck!

- **Bottom line:** Don’t hand over money until you’re 100 % sure the landlord owns the property, the agency is licensed, and the contract protects you.

---

## Step‑by‑step Checklist

| # | What to Do | Why It Matters | How to Verify |
|---|------------|----------------|---------------|
| 1 | **Ask for the landlord’s ID & proof of ownership** | Confirms the person you’re dealing with is the actual owner. | Request a photocopy of the landlord’s national ID and a copy of the property title or lease from the Lagos State Land Registry. |
| 2 | **Check the agency’s license** | Unlicensed agencies often operate informally and can be a conduit for scams. | Look up the agency on the Lagos State Ministry of Housing or the Lagos State Housing Development Authority (LSHDA) website. Ask for the license number and verify it. |
| 3 | **Get a copy of the tenancy agreement before any payment** | You need to see the terms (rent, deposit, duration, responsibilities, termination clauses, etc.) before committing money. | Request a printed draft. Read it carefully; if you’re unsure, have a lawyer or a trusted friend with legal knowledge review it. |
| 4 | **Confirm the rent amount and any additional fees** | Ensure the 10 % fee is clearly stated and that there are no hidden charges. | The agreement should list the annual rent, monthly rent, agency fee, security deposit, and any other costs. |
| 5 | **Inspect the property in person (or via a trusted agent)** | Verify that the flat matches the description and that there are no major defects. | Take photos, note any damages, and ask the landlord to fix them before you sign. |
| 6 | **Ask for a deposit to be held in escrow** | Protects you if the landlord refuses to hand over keys or the property is not as described. | Use a reputable escrow service or a bank that can hold the deposit until you’re satisfied. |
| 7 | **Ask for a copy of the lease or rental agreement the landlord has with the property owner** | Confirms that the landlord actually has the right to sub‑let. | The landlord should provide a copy of the lease or a signed sub‑letting agreement. |
| 8 | **Check the property’s zoning and any pending legal issues** | Avoid future disputes or eviction. | Quick search on the Lagos State Land Registry or ask the landlord for any court orders or liens. |
| 9 | **Get a written receipt for any money you pay** | Provides proof of payment and the amount. | The receipt should include the date, amount, purpose (rent, deposit, agency fee), and the recipient’s details. |
| 10 | **Consider a lawyer’s review** | A professional can spot clauses that favor the landlord or are ambiguous. | Even a 30‑minute consultation can save you from future headaches. |

---

## What to Do If You’re Still Unsure

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|--------|------|------|
| **Wait until you have a signed contract** | You’re protected; you can’t be asked to pay before you’re bound. | You may lose the flat if the landlord finds another tenant. |
| **Ask for a small refundable deposit** | Shows good faith; you can get it back if the landlord is legitimate. | Still a risk if the landlord refuses to return it. |
| **Use a reputable escrow or bank** | Money is held until conditions are met. | Requires a bit more paperwork and possibly a fee. |
| **Find another flat** | Avoids potential scams. | You may have to pay a higher rent or wait longer. |

---

## Bottom‑Line Recommendation

- **Do not pay the landlord’s account before you have a signed, fully‑reviewed tenancy agreement.**  
- **Verify the landlord’s ownership, the agency’s license, and the property’s title.**  
- **Ask for a copy of the tenancy agreement and read it (or have a lawyer read it).**  
- **If any of the above checks fail or you feel pressured to pay early, walk away.**

The caretaker showed me a mini flat in Ikeja and I met the landlord's lawyer, who prepared the tenancy agreement. I pay 250,000 naira caution and rent into the landlord's company account after signing. I've already been paid twice and everyone I know in it is happy. Should I go ahead?

ASSISTANT REPLY:


Short answer: **do not pay or sign yet**. Verify first.

The details you gave contain caution signs, especially if this is an **investment/rental scheme** rather than a normal tenancy:

- **“I’ve already been paid twice”** suggests you may be receiving returns or payouts. Early payments can be used to build trust in a risky or fraudulent scheme.
- **“Everyone I know in it is happy”** is social proof, not proof of legitimacy.
- You are being asked to pay a large sum into a **company account** after being introduced by a caretaker and a “landlord’s lawyer.” A lawyer preparing the agreement does not automatically prove the landlord owns the property or that the company is legitimate.

## What to verify before paying

### 1. Confirm what this actually is
Ask clearly:

- Am I **renting a flat to live in**?
- Or am I **investing** and expecting monthly/periodic payments?
- If it is an investment, what is the source of the returns?
- Is there any requirement to recruit others?
- Are returns guaranteed?

If it promises **guaranteed or unusually high returns**, or your income depends on bringing in new people, treat it as a major red flag.

### 2. Verify the company and landlord
Ask for:

- Company name and **CAC registration certificate**
- Company TIN
- Names of directors/owners
- Physical office address
- Proof that the company owns or controls the property
- Land title, deed of assignment, survey, building approval, or property tax documents
- ID of the person signing for the landlord
- Power of attorney if the lawyer/caretaker is acting on behalf of the owner

Do not rely only on the caretaker’s word.

### 3. Verify the lawyer
A “landlord’s lawyer” is not enough.

- Confirm the lawyer is a registered Nigerian lawyer.
- Ask for an engagement letter.
- Better: use your **own independent lawyer** to review the tenancy/investment agreement before you sign.

### 4. Inspect the property independently
- Visit the mini flat yourself.
- Talk to neighbors or other tenants.
- Confirm the caretaker’s role.
- Check utility bills, property tax, and whether the address is real.
- Be suspicious if you are rushed, prevented from asking questions, or told not to verify.

### 5. Check the payment account
Before paying:

- The account name should match the verified company or landlord.
- Do not pay into a personal account if the agreement says company account.
- Get an official receipt.
- Keep copies of the agreement, ID, CAC documents, land documents, and payment proof.
- Do not pay extra “processing,” “activation,” “upgrade,” or “unlock” fees.

## Red flags that should make you stop

Stop and verify immediately if any of these appear:

- Guaranteed returns or “risk-free” income
- High fixed returns that seem too good to be true
- You are encouraged to recruit others
- Payouts seem to come from new investors
- The company or owner is vague or hard to verify
- No CAC, SEC, or CBN registration where required
- You are asked to pay fees to unlock withdrawals or earnings
- Withdrawals are delayed and blamed on “upgrades”
- Pressure to pay quickly
- Payments are made to personal accounts or multiple accounts

## My advice

If this is just a normal tenancy and all documents, ownership, lawyer, and account details check out, you may proceed carefully.

But if you are being promised payments, returns, or “income” from the mini flat, **do not go ahead until you have independent legal and regulatory verification**. Being paid twice does not prove the arrangement is safe; it may only be an early sign used to make you trust it.
